gap: B breaks the body column: heading words start at x=224 for H1/H2 but x=226 for H3-H6, a hard 2px step between H2 and H3 (row lefts step 26,24,26,26,26 px rather than a uniform 26), so the six headings sit on two columns and the right ragged edge splits with them (609 vs 611); A holds all six on one column at ink-left 223 with 0.52px centroid spread.
gapTheirs: A's grid is fractional and rounds per glyph and per line: cell 25.6px, line 73.6px, so the six-glyph `######` fence's pitch alternates 26/25/26/25/26px instead of B's dead-even 26px, and the cap-top pitch runs 74/73/73/73/73px against B's flat 74px — the picket fence's gaps breathe unevenly and the baseline rhythm is 1px inconsistent where B's is exact.
verdict: This state exists to prove one thing — that six different `#` runs hang out into the gutter and still drop their words on a single column — and B fails it by 2px starting at H3, which means typing a third `#` shoves the whole line right under your caret. A's compensation is uglier under a loupe: a fractional 25.6px cell that rounds per glyph, so the `######` fence's gaps stutter 26/25/26/25 and the line pitch wobbles 74/73. But a stuttering gutter is a wobble in the margin, while a split body column is a wobble in the sentence you are reading. A wins because the column that carries the words does not move.

states.gap: Tighter measure: A's monospace cell is 26.0px vs B's 25.56px, so the same 20-char body line runs to x=731 instead of x=722 — only 49px of right margin in a 780px frame (~21.3 chars of measure vs B's 21.7) before the line has to wrap.
states.gapTheirs: B sets the `######` run in the heading's bold weight — 38.0% ink coverage in the 160×42 gutter box vs A's 25.7% (normalized to each side's own fill, so this is weight, not colour) — making the six hashes the densest object in the whole frame, heavier than the heading word they annotate (29.7%).
states.verdict: Structurally these are the same design: both hang the `######` run at x=43, both land the heading word and the `>`, `-` and `1.` rows on the 225px body column within 1px, and neither draws a rule beside the quote. What separates them is that B renders the hash run bold — 38.0% vs 25.7% ink — so the gutter out-shouts the heading and you scan the marker run before you scan the words. A's markers dissolve on a glance down the draft and leave 'H6 heading here'; B's leave a black bar you have to count. Both then blow 29% of a 780px viewport (225px) on gutter and hand the writer a ~21-character measure, which neither has solved.
secondary: Cell grid: A's advance is an exact 26.0px (gutter offset 182px = exactly 7 cells); B's is 25.56px, so its 182px offset is ~7.08 cells — the hash run is ~2px off its own character grid

Block markers `>` `-` `1.` are regular weight in both (17.9% vs 20.7% normalized ink); only the heading run diverges
